title: Information Theory
body:
[[Entropy]]
$$
I(x) = -\log_{2}\left(P(x)\right)
$$

---

Shannon, 1948. The mathematics of **how much a message tells you**, built entirely on the formula
above and the expectation of it. It shows up in this course for one specific reason:
[[Cross-Entropy Loss]] is the standard [[Classification]] loss, and it is an information-theoretic
quantity rather than an arbitrary formula, so the block exists to say where it comes from.

The whole ladder, in the order it has to be read:

| Quantity | Formula | Reads as |
|---|---|---|
| [[Information]] | $-\log_2 P(x)$ | surprise at one outcome |
| [[Shannon Entropy]] | $-\sum_x P(x)\log P(x)$ | average surprise under $P$: the best achievable code length |
| [[Cross-Entropy]] | $-\sum_x P(x)\log Q(x)$ | code length you get using $Q$ when truth is $P$ |
| [[KL Divergence]] | $\sum_x P(x)\log \frac{P(x)}{Q(x)}$ | the excess, $H(P,Q) - H(P)$ |

Every one of them is an **expectation over $P$**, the true distribution, of something. That is the
single fact that makes the four collapse into one idea; see [[Random Variable]] in [[STATISTICS]]
for what $\mathbf{E}[\cdot]$ means.

**The coding interpretation is what makes it concrete.** Assign each outcome a codeword of about
$-\log_2 Q(x)$ bits. If your $Q$ matches reality, the average message costs $H(P)$ bits and no
scheme does better, which is Shannon's source coding theorem. If your $Q$ is wrong you pay
$H(P,Q)$, and [[KL Divergence]] is precisely the penalty for being wrong. Compression and
learning turn out to be the same problem: a model that predicts well is a code that compresses
well.

The other side of Shannon's work, channel capacity and coding for noise, is where
[[Error Correcting Code]] comes from. That is a different chapter and the vault has it under
`Books/`.

## Why the course cares

Training a classifier means making the model's predicted distribution $Q$ match the true one $P$.
The natural measure of "these two distributions disagree" is [[KL Divergence]], and since $H(P)$ is
fixed by the data and does not depend on your [[Weights]], **minimising KL divergence is exactly
minimising [[Cross-Entropy]]**. That is the derivation of the loss function, and it is why
[[Cross-Entropy Loss]] rather than something else.
